clinicalScope: Hyperplasia – benign increase in cell number in adult tissues, focusing on endometrial hyperplasia and benign prostatic hyperplasia in adult patients seen in low‑resource East African hospitals.
title: Hyperplasia
subject: Pathology
summary: Hyperplasia is a reversible rise in cell numbers that enlarges an organ. It can be normal, like breast growth in pregnancy, or pathological, such as endometrial hyperplasia causing abnormal bleeding or benign prostatic hyperplasia causing urinary obstruction.

sections.p: Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue, leading to organ enlargement. It is classified as:
b: Physiological (e.g., hormonal breast changes, liver regeneration)
Compensatory (e.g., renal tubular hyperplasia after nephrectomy)
Pathological (e.g., endometrial hyperplasia, benign prostatic hyperplasia)
Hormone‑driven vs. growth‑factor driven subtypes

sections.p: Pathological hyperplasia arises when a persistent stimulus drives cell proliferation.
b: Endometrial hyperplasia – unopposed estrogen, obesity, PCOS, estrogen‑only HRT, tamoxifen
Benign prostatic hyperplasia – ageing, androgen exposure, metabolic syndrome, chronic prostatitis
Chronic inflammation (e.g., schistosomiasis of bladder) can trigger hyperplastic response
Nutritional deficiencies (iron, vitamin A) may impair compensatory hyperplasia

sections.p: The stimulus activates intracellular signalling that pushes quiescent cells into the cell cycle.
b: Estrogen binds ER → ↑ cyclin D1 → G1‑S transition in endometrial glands
Androgens → AR‑mediated growth factor release (FGF, IGF) in prostatic stroma
Inflammatory cytokines (IL‑6, TNF‑α) amplify stromal proliferation
Removal of the stimulus leads to apoptosis and regression

sections.p: Visible organ changes reflect the cellular expansion.
b: Endometrium: thickened, often >12 mm on ultrasound, irregular surface
Prostate: symmetrically enlarged, smooth capsular bulge, median lobe protrusion
Liver (compensatory): nodular surface after partial hepatectomy
Kidney (compensatory): enlarged cortex in solitary kidney
Endometrial hyperplasia – increased gland‑to‑stroma ratio, crowded glands, no atypia (simple) or atypia (complex)
BPH – proliferation of both glandular epithelium and stromal smooth muscle, preserved basal cell layer
Absence of infiltrative growth, necrosis, or marked nuclear pleomorphism
Reversible mitotic figures without loss of polarity

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the organ’s function being altered by excess tissue.
b: Endometrial hyperplasia – abnormal uterine bleeding, intermenstrual spotting, infertility
BPH – nocturia, weak stream, incomplete emptying, urinary retention
Compensatory liver hyperplasia – usually asymptomatic, may present with abdominal fullness after surgery
Renal hyperplasia – polyuria if tubular mass interferes with concentrating ability

sections.p: Tests confirm the type and severity of hyperplasia.

t.b: Is endometrial thickness abnormal? → Thickness >12 mm in a post‑menopausal woman suggests hyperplasia
Is estrogen excess present? → Elevated estradiol supports hormonal driver of endometrial hyperplasia
Is prostate enlargement palpable? → Firm, smooth, symmetric enlargement suggests BPH
Is PSA markedly raised? → PSA <4 ng/mL supports BPH; higher values prompt cancer work‑up
What is the histologic pattern? → Simple hyperplasia without atypia vs. complex atypical hyperplasia guides management

sections.p: Pathological hyperplasia is graded to predict malignant potential.
b: Endometrial hyperplasia: simple vs. complex; with vs. without atypia (WHO 2014)
BPH: not staged; severity assessed by International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and prostate volume
Complex atypical endometrial hyperplasia carries ~30 % risk of progression to carcinoma
Low‑grade BPH rarely progresses to cancer but may cause obstructive complications

sections.p: If untreated, hyperplasia can lead to organ dysfunction or malignancy.
b: Endometrial hyperplasia → endometrial carcinoma (especially atypical type)
BPH → acute urinary retention, recurrent urinary tract infection, renal impairment
Compensatory hyperplasia – generally benign, but may mask underlying neoplasm
Overall prognosis good when stimulus removed early

sections.p: Management targets the underlying stimulus, reduces tissue bulk, and relieves symptoms.
b: Endometrial hyperplasia – progestin therapy (oral medroxyprogesterone acetate or LNG‑IUS) to oppose estrogen, weight loss, treat PCOS, stop estrogen‑only HRT
BPH – α‑blockers (e.g., tamsulosin) for smooth‑muscle relaxation, 5‑α‑reductase inhibitors (finasteride) to shrink glandular component, consider minimally invasive surgery if severe
Compensatory hyperplasia – treat underlying loss (e.g., liver support after resection) and monitor for regeneration
Avoid estrogen‑only therapy in women with risk factors; avoid anticholinergics that worsen urinary retention in BPH

sections.p: Linking bedside findings with tissue changes improves diagnostic confidence.
b: A post‑menopausal woman with 15 mm endometrial stripe on ultrasound and obesity likely has estrogen‑driven hyperplasia
A 68‑year‑old man with IPSS 22, enlarged smooth prostate on DRE, and PSA 3 ng/mL fits BPH rather than cancer
Histology showing crowded glands without atypia confirms simple endometrial hyperplasia, guiding progestin use
Stromal overgrowth on prostate biopsy predicts better response to 5‑α‑reductase inhibition

sections.p: A structured answer demonstrates integration of history, exam, investigations and management.
b: Start with targeted history (bleeding pattern, urinary symptoms, hormonal exposures)
Perform focused exam (pelvic exam or DRE) and note organ size
Select the most informative, locally available test first (ultrasound, DRE, symptom score)
Explain why a drug class is chosen and why alternatives are avoided
Outline follow‑up: repeat imaging/biopsy after 3–6 months for endometrial hyperplasia, monitor IPSS and post‑void residual for BPH

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden heavy uterine bleeding causing hemodynamic instability
Acute urinary retention with pain or fever
Rapidly rising PSA >10 ng/mL or hard nodular prostate on DRE
Severe abdominal pain with signs of peritonitis after liver resection

faq.a: Yes, especially atypical endometrial hyperplasia, which has a significant risk of progressing to carcinoma if not treated.

faq.q: Is BPH the same as prostate cancer?
faq.a: No. BPH is a benign enlargement of the prostate gland; cancer shows irregular, hard nodules and markedly elevated PSA.

faq.q: Why stop estrogen‑only therapy in a woman with abnormal bleeding?
faq.a: Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial proliferation; adding progestogen or stopping estrogen removes the stimulus and allows regression.

exam: A 52‑year‑old woman with obesity presents with irregular vaginal bleeding; what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Transvaginal ultrasound to assess endometrial thickness; >12 mm warrants biopsy.

Explain how unopposed estrogen leads to endometrial hyperplasia at the cellular level. — Estrogen‑ER binding up‑regulates cyclin D1, pushing glandular cells from G0 into S phase, increasing gland‑to‑stroma ratio.

Why is a progestin‑releasing intrauterine system preferred over oral progestins in some women with endometrial hyperplasia? — Provides high local progesterone with minimal systemic side effects and improves compliance.
List two reversible causes of compensatory hepatic hyperplasia after partial hepatectomy. — Residual liver mass and growth‑factor surge (HGF, IL‑6); adequate nutrition supports regeneration.
A patient with BPH develops acute urinary retention. What immediate intervention is required? — Insert a Foley catheter for bladder decompression, then plan definitive BPH therapy.
Differentiate simple from complex endometrial hyperplasia on histology. — Simple: mild gland crowding, normal architecture; Complex: marked crowding, irregular gland shapes, possible atypia.

What laboratory test is least useful for diagnosing BPH in a low‑resource setting and why? — PSA, because it may be unavailable and does not change initial management; symptom scores and DRE are sufficient.
How does chronic schistosomiasis of the bladder illustrate compensatory hyperplasia? — Persistent irritation leads to urothelial hyperplasia, increasing bladder wall thickness.

A woman on tamoxifen develops abnormal uterine bleeding. Explain the pathophysiology and management. — Tamoxifen acts as estrogen agonist on endometrium, causing hyperplasia; stop tamoxifen, evaluate with ultrasound, and treat with progestin if hyperplasia confirmed.
